title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $G$ be a geometrically finite Kleinian group with parabolic elements and $f_{G}$ be the associated Markov map. Suppose $G$ has an even-cornered fundamental
	domain $\mathcal{F}$ and let $P$ denote the finite set of all parabolic vertices of $\mathcal{F},$ and define $\mathcal{P}:=\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty} f_{G}^{-n}(P),$ which is the set of all parabolic fixed points of $G.$ Then for each $p\in P,$
	we can choose a sufficiently small neighborhood $U_p$ of $p$ such that the first return map $f_K$ induced by $f_{G}$ on $K$
	is eventually expanding, where
	$$K:=\Lambda(G)\setminus
	\left(
	\bigcup_{p\in P}U_p\;\cup\;\mathcal{P}
	\right)
	\subset \Lambda_c(G).$$

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $G$ be a geometrically finite Kleinian group with parabolic elements and $f$ be the associated Markov map.  Then for every quasiconformal map $g\colon \mathbb{S}^{2}\to\mathbb{S}^{2}$ being compatible
	with $G,$ there exists a neighborhood $U_p$ , for each $p\in P$, such that the set \begin{align}
		K=\Lambda(G)\setminus
		\left(
		\mathcal{P}\cup\bigcup_{p\in P}U_p
		\right)
	\end{align}
	satisfies $\dim_H g(K)=\dim_H g\bigl(\Lambda(G)\bigr),$
	where $P$ denotes the finite set of parabolic vertices of an even-cornered fundamental domain for $G,$ $\mathcal{P} =\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty} f^{-n}(P)$ denotes the set of all parabolic fixed points of $G, $ and $\dim_H$ denotes the Hausdorff dimension.

title: Lemma
body_md:
(Mass distribution principle)
	Suppose $E$ is a compact set and $s\ge 0.$ If there is a mass distribution $\mu $ on $E$ and a constant $C>0$ such that for any $r > 0$,
	$\mu \left ( V \right )\le C \text{diam}( V  )^{s}   $ for all closed sets $V$ with $\text{diam}( V  )\le r ,$ then  dim$_{H}\left ( E \right ) \ge s$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
(The global measure formula,\cite{BO}\cite{VA}) For all $x\in \Lambda \left ( G \right )  $ and all positive $t> 0$, the quantity
	\begin{align}
		\mu _{\delta }  \left ( S\left ( x,t \right )  \right ) exp\left ( -t\delta -\rho \left ( x,t \right )\left ( \delta -k\left ( x,t \right ) \right )   \right )
	\end{align}
	is bounded from above and below. Here $k\left ( x,t \right ) = k\left ( p \right ) $ if $x_{t}\in H_{p}  $ for some $p$ and $0$ otherwise, and
	$$\rho \left ( x,t \right ) = \inf \left \{ d_{\mathbb{B} }\left ( x_{t},y  \right ) :y\notin H_{p}    \right \} ,$$
	if $x_{t}\in H_{p}  $ for some $p$ and $0$ otherwise. Here $d_{\mathbb B}$ denotes the hyperbolic metric on $\mathbb B^3.$

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $G$ be a non-elementary geometrically finite Kleinian group and $\Lambda(G)$ be its limit set. Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all parabolic fixed points of $G$. Suppose that
	$$P=\{p_1,\ldots,p_m\}\subseteq\mathcal P$$
	is the finite set of parabolic vertices of a fundamental domain. Then, for each $i=1,\ldots,m$, one can choose $t_i>0$ sufficiently large so that
	\begin{align}K^{*}=\Lambda(G)\setminus
		\left(
		\mathcal P\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}S(p_i,t_i)
		\right)
	\end{align}
	satisfies
	$\mu_\delta(K^{*})>0.$
	Furthermore,
	$\dim_H K^{*}=\dim_H\Lambda(G)=\delta.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By applying the global measure formula, we know that, for each $x\in \mathcal{P}$, there exists a constant $C$ such that the Patterson-Sullivan measure $\mu _{\delta } $ of the shadow $S(x, t)$  satisfies
	
	$$\mu _{\delta } ( S( x,t))\le C exp\left ( -t\delta -\rho \left ( x,t \right )\left ( \delta -k(x)  \right )   \right )  ,$$
	where $k\left ( x,t \right ) = k\left ( x \right ) $ if $x_{t}\in H_{x}  $ for some $x\in \mathcal{P}$ and $0$ otherwise, and
	$$\rho \left ( x,t \right ) = \inf \left \{ d_{\mathbb{H} }\left ( x_{t},y  \right ) :y\notin H_{x}    \right \} ,$$
	if $x_{t}\in H_{x}  $ for some $x\in \mathcal{P}$ and $0$ otherwise.
	By Fraser's result ( \cite{JF}, Lemma 3.2), we know that $\rho \left ( x,t \right ) \sim t$ as $t\to \infty ,$ for all point $x\in \mathcal{P}.$
	It is easy to see that   $\mu _{\delta }  \left ( S\left ( x,t \right )  \right )\to 0$  by $ exp\left ( -\left ( 2\delta -k \right )t  \right )\to 0 $ as $ t\to \infty .$
	
	Hence, for any $x\in \mathcal{P}$ and positive $r$, there exists a sufficiently large $t_{x} $ such that for any $t>  t_{x} ,$ $\mu _{\delta }  \left ( S(x,t)  \right ) \le r.$ Thus $\mu_\delta(\{p\})=0.$ Note that the set $\mathcal P$ of all parabolic fixed points is countable. Hence $\mu_\delta(\mathcal P)=0,$ since
	$$\mu_\delta(\mathcal P)
	\leq
	\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\mu_\delta(\{p\})
	=0.$$
	
	
	
	                                                                                                                                                                                                    
	By some easy calculation or see  \cite{JF}, we know that the radius of $S\left ( z,t \right )$ uniformly comparable to $e^{-t} .$ The global measure formula gives $$\mu_\delta\bigl(S(x,t)\bigr)
	\asymp
	e^{-\delta t}
	e^{-(\delta-k(x,t))\rho(x,t)}.$$
	Let \begin{align*}K^{*}=\Lambda(G)\setminus
		\left(
		\mathcal P\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}S(p_i,t_i)
		\right).
	\end{align*}. For each point $p_i\in P$ we can choose a  sufficiently small number $r_{i}$ ,  and  a  sufficiently large number $t_{i}$ such that for $t\geq t_{i},$
	
	$$\mu _{\delta }  \left ( K^{*} \right ) = \mu _{\delta }  \left ( \Lambda(G)\setminus \bigcup_{p_{i}\in P}S(p_i,t_i)
	\right ) \ge 1-\sum_{p_{i} \in P}^{}\mu _{\delta }  \left ( S(p_i,t)  \right )\ge  1- \sum_{p_{i} \in P}r_{i}> 0 .$$
	
	Next we will show $\dim_H K^{*}=\dim_H\Lambda(G)=\delta.$ We consider a Frostman-type estimate.
	
	Notice that $G$ is of divergence type, the associated geodesic flow is ergodic by the Hopf-Tsuji-Sullivan theorem (\cite{DS3}, Theorem 14). Thus, by the ergodic law for the ray excursion function (\cite{DS3}, Corollary 19), we have
	$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\rho(x,t)}{t}=0
	\quad\text{for }\mu_\delta\text{-almost every }x\in \Lambda(G).$$
	Taking logarithms in the global measure formula and dividing by $(-t),$ we obtain $$\lim_{t\to\infty}
	\frac{\log \mu_\delta\bigl(S(x,t)\bigr)}{-t}
	=\delta.$$
	Setting $l=e^{-t},$ it follows that $$\lim_{r\to0}
	\frac{\log \mu_\delta(S(x,l))}{\log l}
	=\delta$$
	for $\mu_\delta$-almost every $x\in \Lambda(G).$
	
	                                                                                                                                                  
	
	Fixing $s<\delta$, for $\mu_\delta$-almost every $x\in K^{*}$, there exists $l_x>0$ such that for every $0<l<l_x,$
	$$\frac{\log\mu_\delta(S(x,l))}{\log l}>s.$$
	Whenever $0<l<1$, this inequality is equivalent to
	$$\mu_\delta(S(x,l))\leq l^s.$$
	For each positive integer $n$, define
	$$K_n= \left\{ x\in K^{*}:
	\mu_\delta(S(x,l))\leq l^s \text{ for every }0<l<\frac1n
	\right\}.$$
	Note the fact that
	$$\mu_\delta\left(
	K^{*}\setminus\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}K_n
	\right)=0$$
	and $\mu_\delta(K^{*})>0$, there exists some positive integer $n$ such that $\mu_\delta(K_n)>0.$ Define the normalized restricted measure as
	$$\nu(A)=
	\frac{\mu_\delta(A\cap K_n)}
	{\mu_\delta(K_n)}.$$
	Then $\nu$ is a probability measure supported on $K_n$.
	
	Fix point $y$. For $0<l<\frac1{2n},$ if $S(y,l)\cap K_n=\varnothing,$ then $\nu(S(y,l))=0.$ Otherwise choose point $\xi\in B(y,l)\cap K_n.$
	Then $B(y,l)\subseteq B(\xi,2l).$ Notice that
	and $\xi\in K_n$, we have
	$$\mu_\delta(S(x,2l))\leq(2l)^s.$$
	
	
	Therefore,
	$$\begin{aligned}
		\nu(S(y,l))=
		\frac{\mu_\delta(S(y,l)\cap K_n)}
		{\mu_\delta(K_n)}
		\leq
		\frac{\mu_\delta(S(x,2l))}
		{\mu_\delta(K_n)}
		\leq
		\frac{2^s}{\mu_\delta(K_n)}l^s.
	\end{aligned}$$
	Thus, there exists a constant
	$C_s=\frac{2^s}{\mu_\delta(K_n)}>0$
	such that
	$\nu(S(y,l))\leq C_s l^s$
	for all sufficiently small $l>0$.
	
	Hence by the mass distribution principle (Lemma 3.3), we have $\dim_H K_n\geq s.$
	It follows that $\dim_H K^{*}\geq s,$ since $K_n\subseteq K^{*}.$
	Letting $s$ tend to $\delta$, we have
	$\dim_H K^{*}\geq\delta.$
	On the other hand, $K^{*}\subseteq\Lambda(G)$ shows
	$$\dim_H K^{*}\leq\dim_H\Lambda(G).$$
	
	In conclusion, we have $\dim_H K^{*}=\delta=\dim_H\Lambda(G).$

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $G$ be a geometrically finite Kleinian group with cusps.  Let $ P_{1}$ be the subset of Markov access space $\mathcal{AP}$ which contains all the parabolic period point of $f.$  Then for any $p\in P_{1}$ with period $r,$ there exists a sufficiently small repelling petal region $V_{rep, p}  $ of $p$ and a positive constant $B\left ( V_{rep,p}  \right ) $ such that
	$$\left | \left ( f^{rm_{V}\left ( z \right )  }  \right )^{ '}\left ( z \right )   \right | _{\sigma }> \frac{B\left ( V_{rep, p}   \right ) }{\left | z- p \right |_{\sigma }  } \:\:\:\  for  \:all \:z\in V_{rep,p} , $$ where $m_{V}\left ( z \right )= \min \left \{ m\ge 0:f^{rm}\left ( z \right )\notin V_{rep,p}   \right \} .$

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose  $p$ is an $r$-periodic point of $f,$ i.e. $p=f^{r}\left ( p \right )$ is a fixed point of $f^{r}.$
	Note that $p$ is also a parabolic fixed point of the Kleinian group $G.$ By conjugating $G$ with some M\"obius transformations,  we  can assume $p=\infty$  and the  parabolic element $T_{\lambda }(z)= z+\lambda,\: \lambda\ne 0 $ fixing $p$ is in $G.$
	
	
	By the construction of the Markov map and the definition of the accesses corresponding to $p$, after shrinking the cusp neighborhood, the return map branch $f^r$ coincides with $T_\lambda^{-1}$.  Hence for sufficiently large $|z|$, we have $f^{r}(z)=T^{-1}(z).$
	By the inversion transformation $\eta( u)=\frac{1}{u},$ the local behaviour of $f^{r}$ near $p$ can be represented as the local property of $F=\eta\circ f^{r}\circ\eta^{-1}(u)$ near $0.$ By some easy calculation, we know   $F(u)=\frac{u}{1-\lambda u} $ in a neighbourhood $0.$
	The Taylor expansion of the parabolic rational mapping $F$ near $0$ is $$F\left ( u \right ) = u+\lambda u^{2} +O\left ( u^{3}  \right ) .$$
	Hence $u$ has one attracting petal region and one repelling petal region near $0$.
	
	We can have a sufficiently small neighborhood
	\begin{align} V_{R,H} = \left \{ u:\mathfrak{Re}(\alpha(u))> R,\left | \mathfrak{Im}(\alpha(u))  \right |< H   \right \}
	\end{align} of $0$ in the repelling petal of $F$ by taking sufficiently large $R$ and $ H$
	to ensure that $V_{R, H}\cap K= \emptyset $ and for different $p,q\in P,$ $\overline{V}_{rep,p} \cap \overline{V}_{rep,q} = \emptyset ,$	
	where $\mathfrak{Re}(\alpha(u))$ denotes the real part of $\alpha(u)$ and $\mathfrak{Im}(\alpha(u))$ denotes the imaginary part of $\alpha(u).$
	It is easy to see that $V_{R,H}$ is a sufficiently small region of $0,$ denoted by $V_{rep,0}=V_{R,H}.$
	According to the Parabolic Linearization Theorem (see \cite{MJh}), we know that there is one and, up  to composition with a translation of $\mathbb{C}$, only one conformal embedding $\alpha:V_{rep, 0}\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ which satisfies the Abel function equation $\alpha(F^{(-1)}(u))=1+\alpha(u).$ A simple calculation yields $\alpha(u)=\frac{1}{\lambda u}.$
	We call $\alpha(u)$ the Fatou coordinate of $u.$ It is easy to see that the Fatou coordinates satisfy $\alpha(\left ( F^{(-m)}\left ( u \right )   \right )) =\alpha(u)+m .$	
	
	
	Note that for $u\in V_{rep,0},$ $F$ is expressed in Fatou coordinates satisfying  \begin{align}
		\alpha\left( F^{m}\left ( u \right )   \right ) =\alpha( u )-m .
	\end{align}
	Hence, let $m_{V}\left ( u \right )= \min \left \{ m\ge 0:F^{m}\left ( u \right )\notin V_{rep,0}    \right \} .$ By translation doing not change the imaginary part, we know that $m=m_{V}$ is the first time at which the trajectory leaves $ V_{rep,0}  ,$ so we have: $$\mathfrak{Re} \left ( \alpha(u) -\left ( m_{V}-1 \right )  \right ) > R \:\:and\:\:\mathfrak{Re}\left ( \alpha(u)-m_{V} \right ) \le R .$$
	Note that $\left \{ u:R-1\le \mathfrak{Re}(\alpha(u))\le R, \left | \mathfrak{Im}(\alpha(u)) \right |   \le H   \right \}  $ is a compact set which is away from  $0.$ Consequently, the derivatives of $\alpha$ on this compact set  have an upper bound. Thus there exists  some $0< C_{1}<\infty  $ such that
	\begin{align}\left | \alpha^{'}\left ( F^{m_{V}}  \right )   \right |\le C_{1}  .\end{align}
	Since $F(u)=\frac{u}{1-\lambda u}$ in a neighbourhood $0,$ we obtain
	$F^{m_{V}} \left ( u \right ) = \frac{u}{1-m_{V}\lambda u} $  for $u$ near $0.$
	Furthermore, note that $$\alpha( F^{m_{V}}\left ( u \right )  ) =\alpha( u )-m .$$
	Thus \begin{align}
		\alpha^{'} ( F^{m_{V}} \left ( u \right )   )\left ( F^{m_{V}}   \right )^{'}\left ( u \right ) = \alpha^{'}(u).
	\end{align}
	We have
	\begin{align} \left ( F^{m_{V}}   \right )^{'}\left ( u \right ) =  \frac{ \alpha^{'} \left ( u \right )  }{\alpha^{'} \left ( F^{m_{V}} \left ( u \right )  \right )}.
	\end{align}
	By the asymptotic properties of Fatou coordinates: $\left | \alpha ^{'}\left ( u \right )   \right | \sim  \frac{1}{\lambda}\left| u \right |^{-2}  .$
	
	According to (3.13-3.15), there exists $C_{2}> 0$ such that $$\left | \left ( F^{m_{V}}  \right )^{'}\left ( u \right )    \right | \ge C_{2} \left | u \right | ^{-2} .$$
	
	
	
	For any $z\in V_{rep,p},$ observe that the transformation $z=\eta(\left ( u \right )) = 1/u$ and the spherical metric $\sigma = 2\left | \mathrm{d}z \right | /\left ( 1+\left | z \right | ^{2}  \right ) $, we have
	\begin{align}\left | z-p \right | _{\sigma }\sim \left | u \right | \end{align}
	and
	\begin{align}\left | \left ( f^{rm_{V}}  \right ) ^{'}\left ( z \right )   \right | _{\sigma }= \frac{\sigma \left ( F^{m_{V}}\left ( u \right )   \right ) }{\sigma \left ( u \right ) }\left | \left ( F^{m_{V}}  \right )^{'} \left ( u \right )   \right |.
	\end{align}
	Note that $u=\eta^{-1}(z)$ ,there exists a constant $C_{3} > 0$ such that $$\frac{\sigma \left ( F^{m_{V}}\left ( u \right )   \right ) }{\sigma \left ( u \right ) }\ge C_{3} $$
	and
	\begin{align}\left | \left ( f^{rm_{V}}  \right ) ^{'}\left ( z \right )   \right | _{\sigma }\ge C_{3}\left | \left ( F^{m_{V}}  \right )^{'} \left ( u \right )   \right |\ge C_{3}C_{2}\left | z-p \right | _{\sigma }^{-2}   .\end{align}
	Since $V_{\mathrm{rep},p}$ can be chosen sufficiently small, there exists $\delta>0$ such that $$|z-p|_{\sigma}\leq \delta
	\qquad\text{for all }z\in V_{\mathrm{rep},p}.$$
	Hence,  for  $\:all \:z\in V_{rep,p} $, let $B\left ( V_{rep,p}  \right )=C_{3}C_{2}/\delta> 0 $, we obtain $$\left | \left ( f^{rm_{V}\left ( z \right )  }  \right )^{ '}\left ( z \right )   \right | _{\sigma }> \frac{B\left ( V_{rep,p}   \right ) }{\left | z- p \right |_{\sigma }  }. $$

title: Lemma
body_md: Suppose $p\in P$ is a parabolic periodic point of $f$ with period $r$ and $$\mathcal{O} \left ( p \right ) = \left \{ p,f\left ( p \right ),...,f^{r-1} \left ( p \right )   \right \} $$ denotes its periodic orbits. Let $V_{rep,p} $ be a repelling petal neighborhood of $p.$ Then $$\bigcap_{L=0}^{\infty } \left \{ x\in \overline{V}_{rep,p} :f^{jr}\left ( x \right ) \in \overline{V}_{rep,p} ,0\le j\le L    \right \}= \left \{ p \right \}  .$$ Moreover,for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a finite constant $L_{0}\ge 1 $  such that any point in $$C_{\varepsilon } = \left \{ x\in \overline{V}_{rep,p} :\left | x- p \right |_{\sigma }  \ge \varepsilon  \right \} $$ must leave $\overline{V}_{rep,p} $ after at most $L_{0} $ iterations.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $p\in P$ is a repelling periodic point and $V_{rep,p}$ is a repelling petal of $p.$ For every point $x\in \overline{V}_{rep,p} \setminus \left \{ p \right \} ,$ there exists some $L\ge 1$ such that its $L$-th forward image $f^{rL} \left ( x \right ) $ lies outside $V_{rep,p}.$
	Denoting by $F= f^{r} ,$ then for every $x\in \overline{V}_{rep,p} \setminus \left \{ p \right \} ,$ we have  $\left | F^{'} \left ( x \right )  \right | _{\sigma } > 1$ and  $$\left | F\left ( x \right )-p  \right |_{\sigma } =  \left | F\left ( x \right )-F\left ( p \right )  \right |_{\sigma }= \left | F^{'}\left ( \xi  \right )   \right | _{\sigma }\left | x- p \right |_{\sigma }> \left | x- p \right |_{\sigma }.$$
	Note that $F\left ( p \right ) = p,$ we have $$ p  \in \left \{ x\in \overline{V}_{rep,p}  :F^{j}\left ( x \right ) \in \overline{V}_{rep,p} \:\:for\:\:all\:\:j\ge 0  \right \} .$$
	
	Suppose there exists  another point $x\ne p$ in $\overline{V}_{rep,p}  $ such that $F^{j} \left ( x \right ) \in \overline{V}_{rep,p}  $ for all $j\ge 0.$
	Let $d_{j}= \left | F^{j} \left ( x \right )-p  \right | .$ It is easy to see that $d_{j+1}> d_{j} .$
	Furthermore, for any positive integer $j,$  $F^{j} \left ( x \right )$ belong to the compact set $\overline{V}_{rep,p} ,$ we have $$d_{j}\le \max_{x\in \overline{V}_{rep,p} } \left | x- p \right |_{\sigma } < \infty   .$$ Thus the sequence $\{d_{j}\}$ has a limit $d$ as $j\rightarrow\infty.$
	The monotonicity of $d_{j}$ implies that $d\ge d_{0} = \left | x- p \right | _{\sigma } > 0.$
	
	Observe that $\overline{V}_{rep,p}  $ is compact, for the point $x\in \overline{V}_{rep,p} $, $\{F^{j}(x)\}$ has a convergent subsequence $\{F^{j_{l}}(x)\}$ which converge to some  $y\in \overline{V}_{rep,p}  .$
	Thus $$\left | y-p \right |_{\sigma } =\lim_{l \to \infty}\left | F^{j_{l} }\left ( x \right )-p   \right | = d> 0 ,$$ thus $y\ne p.$
	Therefore we have $$\left | y-p \right | _{\sigma } =\lim_{l \to \infty}\left | F^{j_{l+1} }\left ( x \right )-p   \right |=\lim_{l \to \infty}\left | F\left ( F^{j_{l} }\left ( x \right )  \right )-p   \right |  =\left | F\left ( y \right ) -p \right |_{\sigma } ,$$
	
	However, by the expansibility of points in $V_{rep,p}$,    $\left | F\left ( y \right ) - p \right | _{\sigma }>  \left | y-p \right | _{\sigma } .$ This leads a contradiction. Thus there no such point $x\in \overline{V}_{rep,p} \setminus \left \{ p \right \}  $ such that whose forward $F$-orbit remains entirely in $\overline{V}_{rep,p} .$ Consequently, the set $$ \left \{ x\in \overline{V}_{rep,p}  :F^{j}\left ( x \right ) \in \overline{V}_{rep,p} \:\:for\:\:all\:\:j\ge 0  \right \} $$ contains only a point $p.$
	
	Assume that there is $\varepsilon_{0}>0,$  for any  $n\ge 1,$ there exists a point $z_{n} \in C_{\varepsilon } , $ such that $$z_{n} ,F\left ( z_{n} \right ),...,F^{n}\left ( z_{n} \right )\in \overline{V}_{rep,p}   .$$
	Observe that $C_{\varepsilon }$ is compact, after passing to a subsequence, we may assume that $z_{n}\to z_{\ast }.$ So $$\left | z_{\ast }  -p \right |_{\sigma }  \ge \varepsilon > 0.$$
	
	Fix any $j\ge 0.$ Note that $F^{j} \left ( z_{n}  \right ) \in \overline{V}_{rep,p} $ for any positive integer $n.$
	Since $z_{n}\to z_{\ast } $ as $n\rightarrow +\infty,$ it follows that
	$$F^{j} \left ( z_{n}  \right )\to   F^{j} \left ( z_{\ast }  \right )\in\overline{V}_{rep,p}.$$
	We have $F^{j}\left ( z_{\ast }  \right )\in \overline{V}_{rep,p}$ for all $j\ge 0$. However, the only point whose forward orbit can remain in $\overline{V}_{rep,p}$ forever is $p.$ Hence $z_{\ast } = p,$ which contradicts the fact that $z_{\ast} \in C_{\varepsilon } $ and $\left | z_{\ast }-p   \right |_{\sigma }  \ge \varepsilon > 0$  This contradiction leads to a conclusion of the lemma.

title: Theorem
body_md: Let $G$ be a geometrically  Kleinian group acting on the hyperbolic unit ball space  $\mathbb{B}^{3}$ with parabolic elements. Then for the  subset $K$ constructed in Theorem 3.1, the first return map $f_{K}$ induced by the Markov map $f_{G}$ on $K$ is (eventually) expanding.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To prove the theorem we only need to prove the existence of universal constants $M_{0}$ and $C> 1$ such that $\left | \left ( f^{M_{0}}_{K}   \right )^{'} \left ( x \right )   \right |_{\sigma }   \ge  C.$
	
	For every point $x\in K,$ we let $m\left ( x \right ) $ denote the smallest $m> 1$ such that $f^{m} \left ( x \right ) \in K,$ and $f_{K} \left ( x \right ) = f^{m\left ( x \right ) } (x).$ Let  $\mathfrak{R}$ be the Markov partitions for the group $G.$  Recall that $P$ is the set of all parabolic periodic points or a point in the periodic orbit of some parabolic periodic point of $f$. Let $S$ be the set of all strictly pre-parabolic periodic points in $\partial\mathfrak{R}.$ For convenience, we split the parabolic points in \(S\) and \(\mathcal P\) according to their Markov accesses. Thus, the same geometric point corresponding to different Markov accesses is regarded as two distinct points.
	                                                                                                                 
	Note that $f\left ( S\cup P \right ) \subset S\cup P$ and $\left ( P\cup S \right ) \cap K= \emptyset.$ For any $x\in \Lambda _{c} \left ( G \right )$  and for $\eta>1,$ there exists a positive integer $t(x)$ such that the conformal derivative of $f^{t\left ( x \right ) }$ is bigger than $\eta.$ Denoted by $g\left ( x \right )= f^{t\left ( x \right ) }$, we have $\left | g^{'} \left ( x \right )  \right | _{\sigma } \ge \eta > 1.$
	
	Fix a real number $C>1$. For $x\in K$, let $M(x)$ be the smallest positive integer such that the conformal derivative of $f_{K}^{M(x)}(x)$ is bigger than $C$. The existence of such $M(x)$ will be given latter.
	
	In the following, we will  use $g\left ( x \right )$ to partition the $f$ orbits between $x$ and  $f_{K}^{M(x)}\left ( x \right ) $ as
	$$x,\; g(x),\; g^{2}(x),\; \dots,\; g^{j}(x),\; f_{K}^{M(x)}(x),  g^{j+1}(x)\dots.$$
	Here $j$ is the positive integer such that $f_{K}^{M(x)}(x)$ lies between $g^{j}(x)$ and $g^{j+1}(x).$
	
	
	Let $\alpha = \sup\{ \left | f^{'} \left ( y \right )   \right |_{\sigma }   : y\in \Lambda (G)  \} $ which is finite because $\Lambda (G)$ is compact and $f$ is piecewise smooth. Let $N$ be the number of $f-$orbits of $x$ between $f_{K}^{M(x)}\left ( x \right )$ and $g^{j+1}(x)$(later we will show that $N$ is bounded by a constant which does not depend on $x$). Note that $\left | g^{'}\left ( x \right )   \right |_{\sigma } \ge \eta> 1 .$ Then we have
	$$\left | \left ( f^{M(x)}_{K}   \right )^{'} \left ( x \right )   \right |_{\sigma }   \ge \eta^{\,j+1} \cdot \alpha^{-N} \ge \eta^{\,M(x)/N} \cdot \alpha^{-N}.$$
	Hence, for any $x\in K$ and for some $C > 1$, there must exists a sufficiently large $M$ such that $$\left | \left ( f^{M}_{K}   \right )^{'} \left ( x \right )   \right | _{\sigma }  \ge  C > 1,$$  and denotes  the smallest such integer  number $M$ by $M(x).$
	Since for all $0\le k\le j,$ the $f-$orbits of $x$ from $g^{k} \left ( x \right ) $ to $g^{k+1} \left ( x \right ) $ enter $K$ at most $N$ times, and $f_{K}^{M(x)}\left ( x \right ) \in K ,$ we obtain $M(x) \le N(j+1).$
	We only need to show that $M(x)$  and $N$ are bounded constants which do not depend on $x\in K.$
	To do so, just as McMullen did  in \cite{Mc3}, we will divide $\Lambda \left ( G \right ) $ into to two subsets $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$.
	
	First, for each parabolic periodic point $v\in P,$ we take  a repelling petal neighborhood $V_{v} =V_{rep,v}  $ as the proof of Lemma 3.6 does. For any parabolic pre-periodic point $p\in S,$ let $V_{p} $ be a neighbourhood of $p$ satisfying the conditions of Lemma 3.5, and additionally $f\left ( V_{p}  \right ) \subset V_{f\left ( p \right ) } $.
	
	Let $ K_{1}= \bigcup_{p\in S\cup P }^{} V_{p} $ be a subset of $\Lambda(G).$  For every $p\in S\cup P$  and $x\in V_{p},$ let $v = f^{n(p)}(p),$ where $n(p)$ is the smallest integer such that $v=f^{n}(p)$ is a periodic of $f$ with order $r$. Then $f^{n(p)} (x) \in V_{v}$ and let $m=m_{V} (x)$ be the smallest positive integer such that $f^{rm}(f^{n(p)} (x)) \notin V_{v}.$ We have
	
	\begin{align}\left | \left ( f^{rm(y)+n(p)}  \right )^{'} (x)  \right |_{\sigma } = \left | \left ( f^{rm(y)}  \right )^{'} (f^{n(p)}(x))  \right |_{\sigma }\prod_{k=0}^{n(p)-1} \left | f^{'} (f^{k}(x))  \right |_{\sigma }. \end{align}
	
	
	By the Markov property of $f$, for any $x\in V_{p} ,$ we have $f^{n\left ( p \right ) }(x)\in f^{n\left ( p \right ) }(V_{p}) (\subset V _{v} )$. Furthermore, by Lemma 3.6, there exists a constant $B(V_{v})$ such that
	
	\begin{align}\left | \left ( f^{mr}  \right )^{'}\left ( f^{n\left ( p \right ) }(x) \right )    \right | _{\sigma }  \ge \frac{B(V_{v})}{|f^{n\left ( p \right ) }(x)-v|_{\sigma}}. \end{align}
	
	For any $k\in \left [ 0,n\left ( p \right )- 1  \right ] $, by Lemma 3.5, we  obtain
	
	\begin{align}A(V_{f^{k} (p)})= \inf_{ f^{k} (x)\in V_{f^{k}( p)}} \frac{\left | f^{'} \left ( f^{k} (x) \right )  \right | _{\sigma }  \, |f^{k} (x)-f^{k}( p)|_{\sigma}}{|f^{k+1}(x)-f^{k+1}  (p)|_{\sigma}} > 0. \end{align}
	
	
	Substituting (3.20) and (3.21) into (3.19), we obtain
	\begin{align*}&\left | \left ( f^{rm}  \right )^{'}\left ( f^{n(p)}(x) \right )  \right | _{\sigma }\prod_{k=0}^{n(p)-1} \left | \left ( f^{}  \right )^{'}\left ( f^{k}(x) \right )   \right | _{\sigma }\\
		&\ge \frac{B(V_{v})}{|f^{n(p)}(x) - v|_{\sigma}} \prod_{k=0}^{n(p)-1} \frac{A(V_{f^{k}(p)})\, |f^{k+1}(x) - f^{k+1}(p)|_{\sigma}}{|f^{k}(x) - f^{k}(p)|_{\sigma}}\\
		&\ge \frac{B(V_{v})}{|x-p|_{\sigma}} \prod_{k=0}^{n(p)-1} A(V_{f^{k}(p)}).
	\end{align*}
	
	If $n(p)=0,$ then $p=v$ and for any $x\in \overline{V_{v}} -\{v\}$, $\left | \left ( f^{rm}  \right )^{'}\left ( x \right ) \right |_{\sigma } > C_{2}$ for some constant $C_{2}>1$ because $\left | (f^{r} )^{'}(x) \right |_{\sigma } > 1$ on $\overline{V_{v}} -\{v\}.$
	
	
	If $n(p)>0,$ that means $p$ is an orbital point of $v.$
	We take the diameter of $V_{p} $ to be sufficiently small so that the following inequality holds
	$$\operatorname{diam} V_{p} < A(V_{p}) A(V_{f(p)}) \dots A(V_{f^{n(p)-1}(p)})\, B(V_{f^{n(p)}(p)})$$
	and the quantity $\left | \left ( f^{rm+n(p)}  \right )^{'} (x)  \right |_{\sigma }$ is bigger than some constant $\eta>1.$ Hence, for any $x\in V=\bigcup_{p\in S\cup P} V_{p} ,$  we can define $g(x) = f^{t(x)}=f^{rm(x)+n(p)} (x).$
	
	
	In the following we will show that there is an integer $N_{1} $ independent of $x$ so that if $f^{k} (x)\in K$ is on the $f$-orbit between $x$ and $g\left ( x \right ), $ then $rm+n\left ( p \right )< k+N_{1}.$
	
	Observe that if the orbit of a point contains sufficiently many complete period blocks before leaving a neighborhood of the periodic orbit, then that point must be arbitrarily close to the periodic orbit.
	
	Suppose the periodic orbit of a period  point $v$ is $$\mathcal{O} \left ( v \right ) = \left \{ v,f\left ( v \right ),...,f^{r-1} \left ( v \right )   \right \}. $$
	If $x,F(x),\ldots,F^L(x)\in V_v,$ then by Lemma 3.7, for any $\varepsilon>0$ ,  there is  a sufficiently large positive number  $L$ such that $\left | x- v \right |_{\sigma }  < \varepsilon,$ where $F=f^r$.
	More precisely, let $\varepsilon>0$ be given. For $0\le s<r,$  since $f^s$ is continuous at $v,$ there exists $\delta_s>0$ such that if $|x-v|_{\sigma } <\delta_s
	,$ we have $$|f^s(x)-f^s(v)|_{\sigma } <\varepsilon.$$
	Because there are only finitely many phases $s=0,\ldots,r-1,$ we may take $$\delta=\min_{0\le s<r}\delta_s>0.$$
	Therefore, for every $s\in\{0,\ldots,r-1\},$ if $|x-v|_{\sigma } <\delta
	,$ we have $$|f^s(x)-f^s(v)|_{\sigma } <\varepsilon.$$
	By Lemma 3.7, there exists a positive integer  $L=L(\delta,v)$ such that, whenever $x,F(x),\ldots,F^L(x)\in\overline{V_v},$ we have
	$|x-v|_{\sigma } <\delta.$
	Consequently, $$|f^s(x)-f^s(v)|_{\sigma }<\varepsilon.$$
	Note that $f^s(v)\in P,$ it follows that $$dist(f^s(x),P)
	\le |f^s(x)-f^s(v)|_{\sigma }
	<\varepsilon.$$
	
	We now prove that $N_{1} $ must be finite. First, from the condition $f(V_p)\subset V_{f(p)},$ we know that the orbit of any preperiodic point in $p\in S$ cannot enter $K$ before reaching the periodic orbit.
	
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                                
	  
	For any $x\in V_{p},$ recall that $m=m_{V} (x)$ is the smallest positive integer such that $f^{rm}(f^{n(p)} (x)) \notin V_{v}.$ Let $z= f^{n\left ( p \right ) } \left ( x \right ) \in V_{v} $.
	We have $$F^{j} \left ( z \right )= f^{rj} \left ( z \right ) \in V_{v}  \:\:for \:\:all\:\:0\le j< m,$$ where $F= f^{r} .$ Let $k= n(p)+rl+  s,$ where $0\le s< r,$ and suppose that $$f^{k} \left ( x \right ) = f^{s}\left ( F^{l}\left ( z \right )   \right ) \in K .$$
	
	
	Since the orbit does not leave $V_{v} $ until the $m$-th periodic block, starting from $F^{l} \left ( z \right ) ,$ there are at least $m-l$ periodic blocks remaining in $V_{v} .$ That is $$F^{l} \left ( z \right ) ,F^{l+1} \left ( z \right ),...,F^{m-1} \left ( z \right )\in V_{v} .$$
	
	Assume that there is no finite number $N_1,$  Then,  we have $$f^{k} \left ( x \right ) = f^{s}\left ( F^{l}\left ( z \right )   \right ) \to f^{s}\left ( v \right )\in P   $$
	as $k$ tends to infinity.
	
	Hence $dist\left ( f^{k}\left ( x \right ),P   \right ) \to 0.$ Since $\bar{K} $ is compact and $\bar{K} \cap \left ( P\cup S \right ) = \emptyset ,$ it follows from the construction of $K$ that $d_{0}= dist\left ( \bar{K},S\cup P \right ) > 0 .$
	
	If there exists a sufficiently large $L= m-l$ such that some orbit point is still $L$ periods away from the periodic orbit. Take $\varepsilon = \frac{d_{0} }{2} ,$ then $$dist\left ( f^{k}\left ( x \right ),P   \right ) < \varepsilon = \frac{d_{0} }{2} .$$
	Supposing $f^{k}\left ( x \right )\in K,$ we obtain $$dist\left ( f^{k}\left ( x \right ),P \right ) \ge dist\left ( \overline{K},P  \right ) = d_{0} ,$$ which yields a contradiction.
	
	Therefore, if there exists $k> 0$ such that $f^{k}\left ( x \right )\in K  ,$ then it cannot be too far from eventually leaving the domain. Moreover, since the orbit of any preperiodic point in $S$ cannot enter $K$ before reaching the periodic orbit, and
	\begin{align}rm+n\left ( p \right ) -N_{1} < k< rm+n\left ( p \right ),\end{align}
	we conclude that the orbit of $x$ under $f$ can intersect $K$ only during its last $N_1$ iterates. Hence $rm+n\left ( p \right )< k+N_{1},$ which implies that $N_{1} $ is a uniform constant independent of $x$.
	
	This implies that the $f$-orbit between $x$ and $g\left ( x \right )$ hits $K$ at most $N_{1}  $ times. The orbit  intersecting with $K$ is only when it is outside of $U_{v} .$
	
	
	Now let $ K_{2}=\Lambda (G)\setminus  \bigcup_{p\in S\cup P}^{}V_{p}$ and $\widehat J$ denote the accesses space induced by the Markov partition corresponding to $G$. For each access $p\in S\cup P$, choose a one-sided cylinder neighborhood $V_{p} $ of $p$ and denote its closure in $\widehat J$ by $\overline{V}_p^{\,\widehat J}.$
	
	Set $V^{\,\widehat J}=\bigcup_{a\in S\cup P}\overline{V}_a^{\,\widehat J};
	$ $
	W^{\,\widehat J}=\widehat J\setminus V,$
	and  $\overline W^{\,\widehat J}
	=\widehat J\setminus \operatorname{Int}_{\widehat J}V .$
	Suppose that $p\in P$ is a parabolic periodic point and $p_{a} $ is one of its accesses. Since $V_{p_{a} } $ is a one-sided repelling petal based at $p_{a} ,$ its corresponding access endpoint is $p_{a}, $ hence $p_{a} \notin \overline W^{\,\widehat J}.$ All accesses of  rank-one parabolic periodic points (one point has two accesses) and  rank-two parabolic periodic points (one point has four accesses) have been removed. Therefore, no remaining access direction allows points in $W$ to approach $p.$ Equivalently, in the access topology, $\overline W^{\,\widehat J}\cap P=\varnothing .$
	
	The same argument applies to every one-sided access associated with a preperiodic point on the Markov boundary. Indeed, there is no other undeleted access adjacent to that point.
	
	Consequently, no point of $\overline W^{\,\widehat J}$ is a periodic point or a one-sided preperiodic boundary access. In particular, $\overline W^{\,\widehat J}\cap \left ( P\cup S \right ) = \emptyset .$
	
	Fix $x\in \overline W^{\,\widehat J}$  and define
	\begin{align}F_N (x):=\max_{1\le n\le N }\left | (f^n)'(x) \right | _{\sigma } .
	\end{align}
	
	Case 1: If the point $x$ is in $ J_{\mathrm{rad}},$ by the Koebe distortion theorem for inverse branches, $$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\left | (f^n)'(x) \right | _{\sigma } =\infty.$$ Hence there exists \(n(x)\ge 1\) such that $$\left | (f^n)'(x) \right | _{\sigma }>1.$$
	
	Case 2: If the point $x$ is is a nonperiodic preperiodic point.
	Let $n=n(p)\ge1$ be the minimal integer such that $f^n(x)=p$ for some $p\in P.$
	Since $x\notin\partial \mathfrak{R},$ it lies in the interior of an $n$-cylinder $C.$ Note that $$f^n|_C:C\longrightarrow f^n(C)$$
	is a diffeomorphism, let $\phi=(f^n|_C)^{-1}.$
	Then $\phi(p)=x.$
	                                                                        
	By the strict contraction property of nontrivial inverse branches, $\left | \phi^{'} (p) \right |_{\sigma }  <1. $
	We obtain
	$$\left | (f^n)^{'} (x) \right |_{\sigma }
	=\frac1{\left | \phi^{'} (p) \right |_{\sigma }  }
	>1.$$
	
	In conclusion, for every $x\in \overline W^{\,\widehat J},$ there exists $n(x)\ge 1$ such that $$\left | (f^{n(x)})'(x) \right |_{\sigma }  >1.$$ If $\overline W^{\,\widehat J}$ also contains the outer endpoints of $V^{\,\widehat J},$ then either they belong to $ J_{rad }$ or they are among the  pre-parabolic points described above; hence they are  included in these two classifications.
	
	Fix $x\in \overline W^{\,\widehat J},$ and choose $n\left ( x \right ) $ as above. Let
	$\varepsilon_x
	:=
	\frac{\left | (f^{n(x)})'(x) \right |_{\sigma }  -1}{2}>0.$
	The map defined by $y\longmapsto \left| (f^{n(x)})'(y) \right |_{\sigma }$
	is continuous near $x$ in $\widehat J, $ since $\overline W^{\,\widehat J}$ contains no Markov-boundary points.  Hence there exists a relatively open neighborhood $V_x\subset\widehat J$ such that
	$$\left | (f^{n(x)})'(x) \right |_{\sigma } >1+\varepsilon_x,
	\qquad y\in V_x\cap \overline W^{\,\widehat J}.$$
	The family $\{V_x:x\in \overline W^{\,\widehat J}\}$ covers the compact set $\overline W^{\,\widehat J}.$ Choose a finite subcover $ V_{x_1}, V_{x_1}, \cdots,V_{x_s}$ of $\overline W^{\,\widehat J}.$
	
	Set $N_{2} =\max_{1\le i\le s}n_{x_i},
	$ $
	\delta=\min_{1\le i\le s}\varepsilon_{x_i}>0.$
	For any $y\in \overline W^{\,\widehat J},$ choose $i$ such that $y\in V_{x_i}.$ Then, $$\max_{1\le n\le N_{2}}\left | (f^n)'(y) \right |_{ \sigma }
	\ge
	\left | (f^{n\left ( x_i \right ) })'(y) \right | _{\sigma }
	>
	1+\varepsilon_{x_i}
	\ge 1+\delta.$$
	Thus $$\inf_{y\in \overline W^{\,\widehat J}}\max_{1\le n\le N_{2} }
	\left | (f^n)'(y) \right |_{\sigma }
	\ge 1+\delta>1.$$
	This implies that the $f$-orbit between $x$ and $g\left ( x \right )$ hits $K$ at most $N_{2}  $ times.
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
	  
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
	                                                                                                                       
	  
	                                                                             
	  
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     
	  
	  
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                     
	  
	                                                                                                                                                                  
	  
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
	
	In conclusion, for any $x\notin P\cup S ,$  let $N=\max \{N_{1}, N_{2}\}$.
	Then $\left | g^{'} \left ( x \right )  \right |_{\sigma }\ge \eta = \min \left \{ C_{1},C_{2},\lambda    \right \} > 1  $ and the $f$-orbit between $x$ and $g\left ( x \right ) $ hits $K$ at most $N$ times.

body_md:
We can assume, without loss of generality, that $\infty \in \Omega \left ( G \right ) .$
	
	Let  $\mathcal{A} = \left \{ A_{\alpha }  \right \} _{\alpha \in \Pi } $ be the Markov partition $\mathcal{A} = \left \{ A_{\alpha }  \right \} _{\alpha \in \Pi } $ of $K_{reg} $ defined before the theorem.
	
	Suppose the sequence $\alpha = \left ( \omega _{0} ,\omega _{1}  ,...,\omega _{m} \right )$ is admissible, where $\omega _{0} ,\omega _{m}\in \Omega _{K},$ and $\omega _{i}\in \Omega _{U}, 0<  i<  m  .$ By the construction of the Markov partition of $f_K$ on $K,$  we know that $$f_{K} \left ( A_{\alpha }  \right )= B_{\omega _{m} }  \subset K,$$
	where $B_{\omega }=  R_{\omega }\cap \Lambda _{reg}  \: \: \: for\: \: all\: \: \omega \in \Omega .$
	
	Consider an $n$-cylinder of the Markov partition $\left \{ A_{\alpha _{j_{i} } }  \right \}_{\alpha _{j_{i} } \in \Pi }  $ in $K,$ corresponding to an admissible word $j= \left ( \alpha _{j_{0} },\alpha _{j_{1} },...,\alpha _{j_{n-1} } \right ) $ with $$E_{j}= A_{\alpha _{j_{0} }  }  \cap f_{K}^{-1}\left ( A_{\alpha _{j_{1} }  }   \right )\cap ...\cap f_{K} ^{-\left ( n-1 \right ) } \left ( A_{\alpha _{j_{n-1} } }   \right )   .$$
	Since $j$ is admissible, we have $f_{K}^{n} \left ( E_{j}  \right )= f_{K} \left ( A_{\alpha _{j_{n-1} } }  \right ) ,$ and hence $f_{K}^{n} \left ( E_{j}  \right )= B_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } .$ Here $B_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } }$ is the last symbol of an admissible first-return word to $A_{\alpha _{j_{n-1} } } .$
	
	Note that $f_{K}^
	{n}\mid _{E_{j} }  $ is univalent. Assume  $$T_{j,n}= \left ( f_{K}^{n}\mid _{E_{j} }   \right )^{-1}:B_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } \to E_{j}    .$$ Since $T_{j,n}\in G,$ the map $T_{j,n}$ extends to a globally defined biholomorphic automorphism of the Riemann sphere. For any $\omega  \in \Omega _{K} ,$ fix a complex neighborhood $D_{\omega  } $ of $\omega $ satisfying $\overline{B_{\omega } }\subset \operatorname{Int}(D_{\omega  } ).$   We extend the inverse branch $T_{j,n}$ associated with every cylinder of order $n$ terminating at $B_{\omega  }$  univalent to the  domain $D_{\omega  } .$
	
	For partition $\mathcal{A},$ let $\mathcal{A} ^{\left ( n \right ) }$ be the $n$-th order refinement induced by $\Omega .$
	Then for any $E_{j} \in \mathcal{A} ^{\left ( n \right ) } ,$ denote $$g^{\mu}(E_{j})=E_{j}^{\mu},\:\:\text{and}\:\:g^{\mu } \left ( T_{j,n}\left ( B_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } }  \right ) \right )=T_{j,n}^{\mu }\left ( B_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } }  \right ).$$
	Since $\overline{B}_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu } \subset \operatorname{Int}(D_{t_{\left ( j \right ) }  }^{\mu }  ),$ we may choose a piecewise smooth Jordan curve $\ell  _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu  } $ such that $$B_{t_{\left ( j \right ) }  }^{\mu } \subset Int\left ( \ell _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu  }  \right ) ~~\text{and} ~~\overline{Int\left ( \ell _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu  }  \right ) } \subset Int\left ( D_{t_{\left ( j \right ) }  }^{\mu }  \right ) .$$
	
	Let $$d_{t_{(j)}  }^{\mu } = dist\left ( B_{t_{\left ( j \right ) }  }^{\mu } ,\ell _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu  }  \right )> 0 \:\:\: and \:\:\: L_{t_{(j)}  }^{\mu } = length\left ( \ell _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu  }  \right ) < \infty .$$ For $T_{j,n  }^{\mu }:B_{t_{(j)}  }^{\mu } \to E_{j }^{\mu },$ the curve $\ell _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu  } $ depends only on the terminal symbol.
	If two distinct $n$-cylinders $E_{j},E_{k}  $ have the same terminal symbol, namely $t\left ( j \right ) = t\left ( k \right ) ,$ we use exactly the same curve $\ell _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu  } = \ell _{t_{\left ( k \right ) } } ^{\mu  } .$ Let  $\Pi ^{\left ( n \right ) }$ be the index set of the $n$-th cylinders set $\mathcal{A}^{n}.$ Define $$L_{\mu }= \sup _{n\ge 1,j\in \Pi ^{\left ( n \right ) } } \frac{length\left ( \ell _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu  }  \right )}{2\pi dist\left ( B_{t_{\left ( j \right ) }  }^{\mu } ,\ell _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu  }  \right )^{2 }}.$$
	Since $t\left ( j \right ) \in \Omega _{K} $ and $\Omega _{K}$ is finite, it follows that $$L_{\mu }= \sup_{n\ge 1,j\in \Pi ^{\left ( n \right ) } } \frac{L_{t_{\left ( j \right ) }  }^{\mu }}{2\pi \left ( d_{t_{(j)}  }^{\mu } \right )^{2}  }\le \max_{\omega  \in \Omega _{K} }\frac{L_{\omega   }^{\mu }}{2\pi \left ( d_{\omega   }^{\mu } \right )^{2}  } < \infty   .$$
	
	Fix an arbitrary $n$-cylinder $E_j.$ We know that $T_{j,n}^{\mu } :D_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu } \to \hat{\mathbb{C} } $ is a univalent holomorphic map. For any $y\in B_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu },$ the Cauchy integral formula gives $$\left ( T_{j,n}^{\mu }  \right ) ^{'} \left ( y \right ) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\ell _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu }}^{}\frac{T_{j,n}^{\mu } \left ( \zeta  \right ) }{\left ( \zeta -y \right )^{2}  } \mathrm{d}\zeta .$$ The residue theorem implies $$ \int_{\ell _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu }}^{}\frac{1}{\left ( \zeta - y \right )^{2}  } \mathrm{d}\zeta=0.$$
	Hence  for any $y\in B_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu },$  $$\left ( T_{j,n}^{\mu }  \right ) ^{'} \left ( y \right ) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\ell _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu }}^{}\frac{T_{j,n}^{\mu } \left ( \zeta  \right )-T_{j,n}^{\mu } \left ( y \right ) }{\left ( \zeta -y \right )^{2}  } \mathrm{d}\zeta.$$
	Furthermore, for any $\zeta \in \ell _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu }$ and $y\in B_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu },$  we have $$\left | T_{j,n}^{\mu } \left ( \zeta  \right )-T_{j,n}^{\mu } \left ( y \right ) \right | \le \text{diam } \left(T_{j,n}^{\mu } \left ( D_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu } \right )\right )\:\:\:\text {and}\:\:\:\left | \zeta -y \right |\ge d _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu }.
	$$
	Thus
	\begin{align*}\left | \left ( T_{j,n}^{\mu }  \right ) ^{'} \left ( y \right ) \right |  &\le  \frac{1}{2\pi }\int_{\ell _{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu }}^{}\frac{\left | T_{j,n}^{\mu } \left ( \zeta  \right )-T_{j,n}^{\mu } \left ( y \right )  \right | }{\left |  \zeta -y  \right | ^{2}  } \left | \mathrm{d}\zeta  \right |\\
		&\le \frac{L_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu }}{2\pi \left ( d_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu } \right )^{2}  }\text{diam}\left(T_{j,n}^{\mu } \left ( D_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu } \right )\right).
		\\
		&\le L_{\mu }\text{ diam}\left(T_{j,n}^{\mu } \left ( D_{t_{\left ( j \right ) } } ^{\mu } \right )\right).

body_md:
\label{main}
	Let $G$ be a geometrically finite Kleinian group which has an even-cornered fundamental polyhedron.  Then $G$ has Ruelle's property.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $\mu$ is a $G$-compatible Beltrami coefficient. Let $K$ be a subset of the limit set  $\Lambda(G)$ constructed in Theorem 3.1.
	                                                                                                                                                                                            
	                                                                                                                                                                   
	Then the map $f_{K} $ satisfies the Markov properties on $K.$ Hence we can get an iterated system(IFS) $S$ by $f_{K}$.  Conjugating  $S$ by $g^{\mu } ,$ we get an IFS $S_{\mu}$ as
	$$S_{\mu}= \{ \phi_\alpha  ^{\mu} : \phi_\alpha  ^{\mu}= g^{\mu }  \circ \phi_\alpha  \circ (g^{\mu } ) ^{-1},\; \alpha  \in \Pi \}.$$
	Here the countable index set $\Pi$  is induced by the Markov partition $\mathcal{A} =\left \{ A_{\alpha } \right \} $ on $K$ such that for any $A_{j } \in \mathcal{A},$  $f_{K} ^{-1} \mid _{A_{\alpha  } } = \phi _{\alpha  } \mid _{A_{\alpha  } }.$   This establishes a one-to-one correspondence between the Markov partition $\mathcal{A}$ and the countable index set $\Pi.$
	
	Let $\Pi_{n}^{\mu}$  be the  index set of the set of all quasiconformal deformations of the $n$-th cylinder partitions $\mathcal{A}^{(n)}. $ We have
	$$\psi_n^{\mu}(\iota ) = \sum_{j\in \Pi_n^{\mu}} \| (\phi_{j}^{\mu})' \|^{\iota },\qquad n\ge 1$$
	and let $P$ be the topological pressure function
	$$P(\mu,\iota ) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \psi_n^{\mu}(\iota ),\qquad \iota   \in (\theta_{\mu},+\infty),$$
	where $\theta_{\mu} = \inf_{\iota } \{ \iota  : \psi_1^{\mu}(\iota ) < \infty \}.$
	
	If the set of generators of $G_{\mu}$ contains no parabolic elements, then the index set $\Pi$ is finite. Thus $\theta_{\mu}= -\infty$ and the system is regular. Anderson \cite{AR} proved this result for convex co-compact Kleinian groups with an even-cornered fundamental polyhedron. Their method utilizes the existence of a unique zero of the Ruelle zeta function in the complex plane $\mathbb{C},$ which can be represented by the pressure function $P(\mu,\iota ).$ When the set of generators of $G_{\mu}$ contains some parabolic elements, we need the following lemma, for the case of Fuchsian groups see \cite{HZ}.
	
	\begin{lemma} For any $[\mu]\in \mathcal{T}(G),$ we have $\theta_{\mu} = \frac{k_{max}}{2},$ where $k_{max}$ denotes the largest cusp rank. Furthermore the IFS $S_{\mu}$ is regular.
	\end{lemma}
	
	\begin{proof}
		
		Fix $[\mu]\in\mathcal T(G)$. By definition,
		$$\theta_\mu=
		\inf\left\{
		\iota :
		\psi_1^\mu(\iota )<\infty
		\right\},$$
		where
		$$\psi_1^\mu(\iota )
		=
		\sum_{\alpha\in \Pi}
		\left\|(\phi_\alpha^\mu)'\right\|^\iota .$$
		It suffices to prove that
		$$\psi_1^\mu(\iota)<\infty
		\:\:\text{for}\:\:
		\iota>\frac{k_{\max}}{2},$$
		and
		$$\psi_1^\mu\left(\frac{k_{\max}}{2}\right)=\infty.$$
		
		Let $ P_\mu$ be a finite set of representatives of the $G_\mu$-orbits of bounded parabolic fixed points of $G_\mu$. For each $p\in P_\mu$, let $k(p)\in\{1,2\}$ denote the rank of the corresponding cusp, and choose a finite-index subgroup
		$L_p<  \operatorname{Stab}_{G_\mu}(p)$ such that $L_p\cong\mathbb Z^{k(p)}.$
		Set
		$k_{\max}
		=
		\max_{p\in P_\mu}k(p).$
		We decompose the index set $\Pi$ as
		$$\Pi
		=
		\Pi_h
		\cup
		\bigcup_{p\in P_\mu}\Pi_p,$$
		where $\ \Pi_h$ corresponds to the hyperbolic branches and $ \Pi_p$ corresponds to the parabolic branches associated with the cusp $p$. Consequently,
		$$\psi_1^\mu(\iota)
		=
		\sum_{\alpha\in \Pi_h}
		\left\|(\phi_\alpha^\mu)'\right\|^\iota
		+
		\sum_{p\in P_\mu}
		\sum_{\alpha\in \Pi_p}
		\left\|(\phi_\alpha^\mu)'\right\|^\iota.$$
		By the construction of the Markov map $f$ and the definition of the induced map $f_K$, the set $\Pi_h$ is finite \cite{BS}. Hence, for every $\iota\geq0$,
		$$\sum_{\alpha\in\Pi_h}
		\left\|(\phi_\alpha^\mu)'\right\|^\iota
		<\infty.$$
		
		
		For the parabolic case, fix  $p\in\mathcal P_\mu$ and let
		$r=k(p).$
		After  changing  coordinates by Mobius conjugation-transforation, we may assume that $p=\infty$.  Choose $L_p$  to act as a lattice of translations on
		$$\mathbb R^r\subset\mathbb R^2.$$
		The orbit map
		$$\gamma \longmapsto \gamma (0),
		\qquad \gamma \in L_p$$
		identifies $L_p$ with a discrete lattice in $\mathbb R^r$. 	More generally, the cusp stabilizer may also have a finite rotational part acting in the directions orthogonal to $\mathbb R^r$, but this does not affect the convergence of the series considered below.
		By the bounded distortion property of the induced Markov system and the construction of the parabolic branches, with comparison constants independent of $\gamma \in L_p$, we have
		$$\sum_{\alpha\in\Pi_p}
		\left\|(\phi_\alpha^\mu)'\right\|^\iota
		\asymp
		\sum_{\gamma \in L_p}
		|\gamma '(0)|_\sigma^\iota,$$
		where $|\gamma '(0)|_\sigma$ denotes the derivative norm with respect to the spherical metric
		$$ds_\sigma=\frac{2|dz|}{1+|z|^2}.$$
		The spherical derivative of $\gamma $ is given by
		$$|\gamma '(z)|_\sigma
		=
		|\gamma '(z)|
		\frac{1+|z|^2}{1+|\gamma (z)|^2}.$$
		We have $|\gamma '(0)|=1,$ since the elements of $L_p$ act as Euclidean isometry in the above coordinates. Therefore
		$$|\gamma '(0)|_\sigma
		=
		\frac{1}{1+|\gamma (0)|^2}.$$
		Hence
		$$\sum_{\alpha\in\Pi_p}
		\left\|(\phi_\alpha^\mu)'\right\|^\iota
		\asymp
		\sum_{\gamma \in L_p}
		(1+|\gamma (0)|^2)^{-\iota}.$$
		
		Since $\{\gamma (0):\gamma \in L_p\}$ is a full-rank lattice in $\mathbb R^r$, the preceding lattice sum has the same convergence behavior as
		$$\int_{\mathbb R^r}
		(1+|x|^2)^{-\iota}\,dx.$$
		Using polar coordinates, we obtain
		$$\int_{\mathbb R^r}
		(1+|x|^2)^{-\iota}\,dx
		=
		\operatorname{area}(S^{r-1})
		\int_0^\infty
		\frac{t^{r-1}}{(1+t^2)^\iota}\,dt.$$
		As $t\to\infty$, the radial integrand satisfies
		$$\frac{t^{r-1}}{(1+t^2)^\iota}
		\asymp
		t^{r-1-2\iota}.$$
		Thus, the integral, and consequently the corresponding lattice sum, converges if and only if
		$$r-1-2\iota<-1$$
		or equivalently,
		$$\iota>\frac r2.$$
		
		When $\iota=r/2$, the integrand is asymptotic to $t^{-1}$, and hence both the integral and the corresponding lattice sum diverge. Therefore, for every $p\in P_\mu$,
		$$\sum_{\alpha\in\Pi_p}
		\left\|(\phi_\alpha^\mu)'\right\|^\iota
		<\infty
		\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
		\iota>\frac{k(p)}{2}$$
		and
		$$\sum_{\alpha\in\Pi_p}
		\left\|(\phi_\alpha^\mu)'\right\|^{k(p)/2}
		=
		\infty.$$
		Since $ P_\mu$ is finite and the contribution from the hyperbolic branches is always finite, it follows that
		$$\psi_1^\mu(\iota)<\infty
		\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
		\iota>
		\frac12\max_{p\in P_\mu}k(p)
		=
		\frac{k_{\max}}2.$$
		In particular, if $p$ is any cusp of rank $k_{\max}$, then the parabolic contribution diverges at $\iota=k_{\max}/2$. Hence
		$$\psi_1^\mu\left(\frac{k_{\max}}2\right)=\infty.$$
		It follows that
		$$\theta_\mu=\frac{k_{\max}}2.$$
		Finally, by the regularity criterion for countable conformal iterated function systems cited above,
		$$S_\mu\text{ is regular}
		\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
		\psi_1^\mu(\theta_\mu)=\infty.$$
		                         
		                           
		    
		                                          
		    
		            
		Thus the system $S_\mu$ is regular.
		
		
		                                                           
		                                                                                                                     
		    
		                                                                                                                     
		
		                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
		                                                                 
		                                                                               
		                                                                               
		                                                                                                                           
		                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
		
		                                                                                                                                    
		                                                                       
		
		                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
		
		                                                                                                
		                                                                                                              
		                                                                                                                                 
		                                                                                   
		                                                                                
		                                                                                            
		                                                                                                                                                          
		                                                                                                                                                                                                 
		                                                                                                                                                              
		
		                                                                                                                                                                                                            
	\end{proof}
	
	
	Mauldin and Urbanski \cite{MU} showed that, for a regular system, the dimension of the limit set is the unique zero of the function $\iota \mapsto P(\mu,\iota).$ To finish the proof of the theorem, it remains only to prove that the zero varies real analytically with respect to $\left [ \mu  \right ] .$ This follows from the classical thermodynamic formalism (a generalization of the Perron–Frobenius theorem, see \cite{Bo} \cite{Ru}): $\exp P(\mu,\iota)$ is an isolated eigenvalue of a transfer operator. The theorem follows from the implicit function theorem applied to $(\mu,\iota) \mapsto \exp(P(\mu,\iota)).$

body_md:
Let $\delta(r)$ denote the {Poincar$\acute{e}$ } convergence exponent of the Hecke group $\Gamma_{r}.$  The function $\delta(r)$ is real-analytic with respect to $r$ in the interval $(0,1).$
Moreover, $\delta(r)$ can be extended continuously to the closed interval $[0,1].$ Under the self-similar decomposition of the critical conformal measure, $\delta(r)$ satisfies the normalization equation
\begin{align}
1=
2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\left(\frac r{2n}\right)^{2\delta(r)}
a_n(\delta(r)),
\end{align}
where $a_n(\delta(r))$ is the correction factor arising from the distortion of the branches, and $a_n(\delta(r))\longrightarrow 1
$ as $n\to\infty.$ Furthermore, $\delta(r)
=
\frac{1+r}{2}+O(r^2)$ as $r\to 0,$  and if $X_r$ denotes the orientable double cover of $\mathbb H/\Gamma_r,$ then $$1-\delta(r)
\sim
\lambda_0(X_r)
\asymp
\sqrt{1-r} \:\: \text{as}\:\: r\to1.$$

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof will be divided into three parts.

First, we  consider the case $\delta(r) \longrightarrow \frac{1}{2}$ as $r\to 0$  to ensure the continuity of $\delta(r)$ at $0.$ The method we adopted  here is from McMullen (\cite{Mc2}, Theorem 3.6 ).  It can be see that for sufficiently small $r$ , the limit set $\Lambda_r$ is a Cantor set.
After removing the infinity point $\infty$  and its countable orbit under the group action, the limit set can be decomposed into a sequence of connected                                                   branches . Let $\Lambda_r(0)$ denote the basic branch containing the origin, and let $\Lambda_r(n)$ denote the branch concentrated near $2n,$ where $n\in\mathbb Z.$ Then up to a countable set with measure zero, there is a self-similar decomposition $$\Lambda_r(0)
=
\rho_r\left(
\bigcup_{n\ne0}\Lambda_r(n)
\right),$$ where $\rho_r$ is the reflection about the circle $C_r.$

Let $\mu_r$ be a $\delta(r)$ dimension critical conformal measure of $\Gamma_r.$ Since the derivatives of the translations $T_{2n}$ are modulus $1$ in the Euclidean metric,  all the translated branches have the same measure $\mu_r(\Lambda_r(n))
=
\mu_r(\Lambda_r(0)).$
By conformal invariant of the measures $\mu_{r}$, we obtain $$\mu_r(\Lambda_r(0))
=
\sum_{n\ne0}
\int_{\Lambda_r(n)}
|D\rho_r(z)|^{\delta(r)}
\,d\mu_r(z).$$
For sufficiently large $|n|$ and $z\in\Lambda_r(n)$ , the branch $\Lambda_r(n)$ is concentrated near $2n.$ Hence  $|z|\asymp2|n|.$  Furthermore notice that $|D\rho_r(z)|=\displaystyle \frac{r^{2}}{|z|^{2}}$, we have $$|D\rho_r(z)|^\delta
=
\left(\frac r{2|n|}\right)^{2\delta}
\bigl(1+\text{distortion term}\bigr).$$
By the symmetry between $n$ and $-n,$ we obtain the critical normalization equation $$1=
2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\left(\frac r{2n}\right)^{2\delta(r)}
a_n(\delta(r)),$$ where $a_n(\delta(r))\longrightarrow1
,$ as $n\to\infty.$

If we temporarily ignore the branch distortion and set $a_n(\delta,r)\sim 1,$ we obtain the model equation
\begin{align} 1\sim
2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\left(\frac r{2n}\right)^{2\delta}.
\end{align}

Let us consider the Riemann zeta function $$\zeta(s)
=
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^s},
\qquad
\operatorname{Re}s>1.$$ Then (5.2) becomes $1
\sim
2\left(\frac r2\right)^{2\delta}
\zeta(2\delta),$ or equivalently
\begin{align}2\zeta(2\delta)
\sim
\left(\frac r2\right)^{-2\delta}.
\end{align}

Now let  $r\to 0,$ note that  the Riemann zeta function has a unique pole at $s=1,$ it follows that $2\delta(r)\longrightarrow1, $ i.e. $\delta(r)\longrightarrow\frac{1}{2} $ as $r\to 0.$

Note that (5.2) is a asymptotic estimation formula, in the following  we will give a more precise estimation to prove that $\delta(r) = \frac{1+r}{2} + O(r^2) \quad \text{as } r \to 0,$ which is a result of McMullen.

Set $\delta=\frac12+\varepsilon,
$ $ \varepsilon>0.$ For $s$ near $1$, the Riemann zeta function has the Laurent expansion
$$\zeta(s)
=
\frac1{s-1}
+\mathcal{C }_{0}
+O(s-1),$$ where $\mathcal{C }_{0} $ is the Euler-Mascheroni constant defined as
$$\mathcal{C }_{0}
=
\lim_{N\to\infty}
\left(
\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac1n-\log N
\right).$$
Thus \begin{align}\zeta(1+2\varepsilon)
=
\frac1{2\varepsilon}
+\mathcal{C }_{0}
+O(\varepsilon).
\end{align}
Substituting (5.4) into the model equation (5.3), we can have

\begin{align}\frac1{\varepsilon}
+2\mathcal{C }_{0}
+O(\varepsilon)
=
\frac2r
\exp\left(
2\varepsilon\log\frac2r
\right)= \frac{2}{r}\Bigl(1 - 2\varepsilon\ln(r/2) + O(\varepsilon)\Bigr).
\end{align}
Let $\varepsilon = cr + o(r),$ it follows from (5.5) that
$$\frac{1}{cr} + 2\mathcal{C }_{0}  + O(r) = \frac{2}{r}\Bigl(1 - 2cr\ln(r/2) + O(r)\Bigr).$$
Multiplying both sides by $r$, we have
$$\frac{1}{c} + 2\mathcal{C }_{0}  r + O(r) = 2 - 4cr\ln(r/2) + O(r).$$
Note that $r\log\frac1r\longrightarrow0$ as $r\to 0,$ the dominant terms in (5.5) imply $\varepsilon\asymp r,$ which implies $c = 1/2,$ and thus $\varepsilon = \frac{r}{2} + O(r).$
Furthermore, this gives $$\delta(r)
=\frac12+\frac r2+O(r).$$

If we reconsider the error produced by the factor $\exp\left(
2\varepsilon\log\frac2r
\right),$ then the model equation gives $$\delta(r)
=
\frac{1+r}{2}
+
O\left(r^2\log\frac1r\right).$$
However, the complete self-similar equation also contains the  distortion factors $a_n(\delta(r)).$ Therefore the rough model  (5.2) alone does not directly imply an error term $O(r^2)$.
A more precise estimate of the leading eigenvalue of the complete transfer operator is given by McMullen’s eigenvalue method (Theorem 3.6 \cite{Mc2}) which implies  $$\delta(r)
=\dim_{H}(\Lambda_r)
=
\frac{1+r}{2}+O(r^2),
\qquad r\to0.$$
Consequently, after defining $\delta(0)=\frac12,$ the function $\delta(r)$ is continuous at $r=0.$


Second,  we will prove  that $\delta(r) \to 1 \quad \text{as } r \to 1.$

For $r=1,$ the circle $C_1$ is tangent to  $\ell_{+}$ and $\ell_{-}.$ Hence the limit set is $\Lambda_1=\widehat{\mathbb R}$ and $\delta(1)
=
\dim_{H}(\Lambda_1)
=
1.$

Let $r\to 1.$ Since the circles $C_{r}$ converge to $C_1,$ the reflections $\rho_{r}$ in these circles converge to $\rho_1.$  Note that the reflections about the two vertical lines   $\ell_{+}$ and $\ell_{-}$ are  independent of $r.$ Hence the generators converge, and therefore $\Gamma_{r}\longrightarrow\Gamma_1$ algebraically, for the definition of algebraical convergence see \cite{Mc1}.

                     
            
                                                          
                    
             

For $r<1,$ the circle $C_r$ is disjoint from the line $\ell_{+}.$ Hence the product of the reflections in these two geodesics is a hyperbolic element. Let $d_r=d_{\mathbb H^2}(C_r,\ell_{+}),$ denote the hyperbolic distance between the two geodesics. The translation length of the product of the two reflections is $2d_r.$ Consequently, its multiplier is $\lambda_r=e^{2d_r},$ or its reciprocal, depending on the chosen of fixed points.

As $r\to1,$ the circle $C_r$ becomes tangent to $\ell_{+},$ and therefore $d_r\longrightarrow0.$ It follows that $\lambda_r\longrightarrow1.$
Moreover, $\lambda_r$ approaches $1$ along the positive real axis, which is precisely the condition for radial convergence of the accidental parabolic element.

By symmetry, the same argument applies to the geodesic pair $(C_r,\ell_{-}).$ Hence he limiting group arise from the geodesic pairs $(C_1,\ell_{+}), (C_1,\ell_{-})$ contains two accidental parabolic elements.


In \cite{Mc2}, McMullen showed that
if $\Gamma_n\to\Gamma$ algebraically and  all accidental parabolics converge radially, then $\Gamma_n\to\Gamma$ dynamically.
In the present family, all accidental parabolic elements arise from the two tangent pairs described above, and we have verified that they converge radially. Therefore, $\Gamma_{r}\longrightarrow\Gamma_1$ dynamically, which implies $\dim_{H}(\Lambda_{r_j})
\longrightarrow
\dim_{H}(\Lambda_1) \:\:\text{as}\:\: r_{j} \to 1.$
We conclude that $\delta(r)\longrightarrow1,
$ as $ r\to1.$ Thus, after defining $\delta(1)=1,$ the function $\delta(r)$ is continuous at $r=1.$



In order to prove the analytic property, we need a more precise quantitative estimate as $r\to1.$ In the following, we will provide a quantitative estimate for $1 - \delta(r) \sim \lambda_0(X_r) \asymp \sqrt{1 - r} $ as $ \to 1.$
To do so,  we divide the quotient surface into three parts, separating the convex core from the ends of infinite volume.


Let $X_r$ denote the orientate double cover of the quotient surface $\mathbb H/\Gamma_r.$ Consider the convex core of the surface $X_r.$ For $0<r<1,$ it is easy to see that $X_r$ has a geometrically finite hyperbolic pair of pants with one rank-one cusp and two ends of infinite volume. Its convex core, denoted by $\operatorname{Core}(X_r)$,  has finite area. The boundary of $\operatorname{Core}(X_r)$ consists of two simple closed geodesics of equal length, denoted their common length by $L_r.$ Furthermore, the two  geodesics divide $X_r$ into three parts:
$$X_r=
\operatorname{Core}(X_r)
\cup E_r^+
\cup E_r^-,$$ where $E_r^+$ and $E_r^-$ are the two ends of infinite volume.
As $r\to1,$ we can see   $L_r\longrightarrow0$  and the two boundary geodesics degenerate into the two rank-one cusps of the limiting surface.

Denote the bottom of the spectrum of the surface $X_{r}$ by $\lambda_0(X_r).$		The variational characterization of the bottom of the spectrum is
\begin{align}\lambda_0(X_r)
=
\inf_{0\ne f\in C_c^\infty(X_r)}
\frac{\displaystyle\int_{X_r}|\nabla f|^2\,dA}
{\displaystyle\int_{X_r}|f|^2\,dA}.
\end{align}
The bottom of the spectrum of the Laplacian is controlled by the short geodesics. In the following, we will use the standard short-geodesic estimate to give $\lambda_0(X_r)\asymp L_r.$

For the asymptotic estimates at $r\to 1,$ the method we used here is from \cite{Mc2} and \cite{Mc3}.

By McMullen \cite{Mc1} , we know that $\Gamma_r\to\Gamma_1$ converges strongly as $r\to 1.$ Hence the two infinite-volume ends degenerate into two rank-1 cusps. At this point, two accidental parabolic points are generated. These short geodesics control the least eigenvalue of the Laplacian. We have
\begin{align}\lambda_0(X_r)
=
\inf_{0\ne f\in C_c^\infty(X_r)}
\frac{\displaystyle\int_{X_r}|\nabla f|^2\,dA}
{\displaystyle\int_{X_r}|f|^2\,dA}.
\end{align}
since the quotient above is approximately minimized by a function with $f=1$ in $\operatorname{Core}(X_r)$, and $f=0$ in the infinite volume ends, and $\nabla f$ supported in standard collar neighborhoods of the short geodesics, see \cite{JT}.

In the following, we  explain that the areas of standard collar neighborhoods of the short geodesics are controlled by the length of the core curves.
Let $\eta  $ be a simple closed geodesic of length $l.$ The half-width $w(\eta )$ of the standard embedded collar satisfies $$\sinh w(\eta )\,\sinh\frac l2=1.$$
Using Fermi coordinates $(\rho,t),$ the hyperbolic metric in the collar is $d\rho^2+\cosh^2\rho\,dt^2,$ where $-w(\eta )\le\rho\le w(\eta  )$ for $
0\le t\le l.$
Hence the area of the entire collar is
$$\operatorname{Area}(\operatorname{Coll}(\eta  ))
=\int_0^l
\int_{-w(\eta )}^{w(\eta )}
\cosh\rho\,d\rho\,dt.$$
Computing the  integral gives $$\operatorname{Area}(\operatorname{Coll}(\eta ))
= 2l\sinh w(\eta ).$$
Note that $\sinh w(\eta )
=
\frac1{\sinh(l/2)},$ we obtain $$\operatorname{Area}(\operatorname{Coll}(\eta ))
=
\frac{2l}{\sinh(l/2)}.$$
Let $l$ tend $0,$ we have $\operatorname{Area}(\operatorname{Coll}(\eta ))
\longrightarrow 4.$
Thus the area of the collar remains bounded. This allows us to compare the numerator with $L_r.$ In the following we will give the estimation of the asymptotic behavior of the length $L_r$ as $r$ approaching 1.

By symmetry, it suffices to compute the distance between $C_r=\{z\in\mathbb H^2:|z|=r\}$ and the vertical geodesic $\ell_{+}
=\{z\in\mathbb H^2:\operatorname{Re}z=1\}.$




The two boundary endpoints of $C_r$ in $\mathbb{R}$ are $-r$ and $r,$ while the two boundary endpoints of $\ell_{+}$ are $1$ and $\infty.$ By the cross-ratio formula for the distance between two disjoint geodesics in the upper half-plane model, we have $$\cosh d_{\mathbb H^2}(C_r,\ell_{+})
=
\frac{1+r}{2r}.$$
Therefore, $$d_{\mathbb H^2}(C_r,\ell_{+})
=
\operatorname{arcosh}
\left(
\frac{1+r}{2r}
\right).$$
Note that the length of the closed geodesic corresponding to the product of the two reflections is twice the length of the common perpendicular. Hence
\begin{align}L_r
=
2d_{\mathbb H^2}(C_r,\ell_{+})
=
2\operatorname{arcosh}
\left(
\frac{1+r}{2r}
\right).
\end{align}
Observe that $\frac{1+r}{2r}
=1+\frac{1-r}{2r}.$ Set $x=\frac{1-r}{2r}.$ Then by some easy calculations we have
                                                                                          
\begin{align}d_{\mathbb H^2}(C_r,\ell_{+})
\asymp
\sqrt{\frac{1-r}{r}}.
\end{align}
Combining (5.8) and (5.9), we have $$L_r
\asymp
\sqrt{1-r},
\qquad r\to1.$$


                                                                                                                                  

Since $\Gamma_r$ is a non-elementary geometrically finite Fuchsian group with  parabolic elements, its critical exponent satisfies $\delta(r)>\frac{1}{2}.$
By Sullivan's spectral formula and together with the related results of Bishop–Jones and Sullivan \cite{BJ}\cite{DS3}\cite{DS4}, we have $$\lambda_0(X_r)
=
\delta(r)\bigl(1-\delta(r)\bigr).$$

In general, for $M=\mathbb H^{d+1}/\Gamma,$ the bottom of the spectrum satisfies $$\lambda_0(M)
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{d^2}{4},
& \delta(\Gamma)\le\dfrac d2,\\[6pt]
\delta(\Gamma)\bigl(d-\delta(\Gamma)\bigr),
& \delta(\Gamma)\ge\dfrac d2.
\end{cases}$$
Hence for the case of Fuchsian groups ($d=1,$ )
we have $$\lambda_0(X_r)
=
\delta(r)\bigl(1-\delta(r)\bigr)
\sim
1-\delta(r).$$
Thus, $1-\delta(r)
\sim
\lambda_0(X_r).$ On the other hand, $\lambda_0(X_r)\asymp L_r$ and $L_r\asymp\sqrt{1-r}.$
                                                        
 
                                                              
               
Combining these estimates gives $$1-\delta(r)
\sim
\lambda_0(X_r)
\asymp
L_r
\asymp
\sqrt{1-r},
\qquad r\to1.$$
              
 
   
                      
     
               
       
            
              
   
 
                                                                 

Now its time to give the proof of the real analyticity of the Hausdorff dimensions of the limit set $\Lambda(\Gamma_{r})$ for $ r \in (0, 1).$
We firstly construct the Ruelle transfer operator $(\mathcal L_{s,r}u)(x)$ for this group using the group elements.

Fix $r\in(0,1)$. After removing the parabolic fixed points in the limit set and their countable orbits under the group action, the basic branch, denoted by $\Lambda_r(0)$, admits a countable Markov partition. Denote by $\Sigma
=
(\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\})^{\mathbb N}$ the symbolic space
with the left shift map
$$\sigma(n_1,n_2,n_3,\ldots)
=
(n_2,n_3,\ldots).$$
For each $n\ne0$, define the inverse branch by
$$f_{n,r}
=
\rho_r\circ T_{2n},
\qquad
T_{2n}(z)=z+2n.$$
                                                        
For a finite word
$$\omega=(n_1,\ldots,n_k)
\in(\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\})^k,$$
let
$$f_{\omega,r}
=
f_{n_1,r}\circ\cdots\circ f_{n_k,r}.$$
Note that
$|DT_{2n}|=1$
and
$|D\rho_r(z)|
=
\frac{r^2}{|z|^2},$
we have
$$|Df_{n,r}(z)|
=
\frac{r^2}{|z+2n|^2}$$
and
$$|Df_{\omega,r}(z)|
=
\prod_{j=1}^{k}
\left|
Df_{n_j,r}
\left(
f_{n_{j+1},r}\circ\cdots\circ f_{n_k,r}(z)
\right)
\right|.$$
Thus for sufficiently large $|n|$,
$$|Df_{n,r}(z)|
\asymp
\left(\frac r{2|n|}\right)^2.$$
Therefore, for every $s>\frac{1}{2}$,
$$\sum_{n\ne0}
\sup_z |Df_{n,r}(z)|^s
<\infty.$$
For $s>\frac12$, define the Ruelle transfer operator by
$$(\mathcal L_{s,r}u)(x)
=
\sum_{n\ne0}
|Df_{n,r}(x)|^s
u(f_{n,r}(x)).$$
                                                            
 
                                                                                        
Since this system has countably many branches, we use the transfer-operator theory for countable Markov systems rather than the ordinary matrix theory for finite-branch systems. Let $\mathcal L_{s,r}$ act on a suitable space of analytic functions on an appropriate complex neighborhood.
According to Theorem 1.2, the operator family
$$(s,r)\longmapsto\mathcal L_{s,r}$$
is real-analytic in $(s,r)$, and its maximal eigenvalue is a positive, isolated simple eigenvalue. Denote this maximal eigenvalue by $\lambda(s,r).$
Hence there exist a strictly positive eigen-function $h_{s,r}$ and a positive eigen-measure $\nu_{s,r}$ normalized by
$$\int h_{s,r}\,d\nu_{s,r}=1$$ such that
$$\mathcal L_{s,r}h_{s,r}
=
\lambda(s,r)h_{s,r}$$
and
$$\mathcal L_{s,r}^{*}\nu_{s,r}
=
\lambda(s,r)\nu_{s,r}.$$
Define the equilibrium measure
$$\mu_{s,r}
=
h_{s,r}\nu_{s,r}.$$
For a word of length $k$, define the partition function $Z_k(s,r;x)$ as
$$Z_k(s,r;x)
=
\sum_{|\omega|=k}
|Df_{\omega,r}(x)|^s.$$
By the iteration formula for the transfer operator, we have
$$\mathcal L_{s,r}^{\,k}\mathbf1(x)
=
Z_k(s,r;x).$$
According to the Ruelle-Perron-Frobenius theorem,
$$Z_k(s,r;x)
=
\lambda(s,r)^k
\bigl(h_{s,r}(x)+o(1)\bigr),$$
where the error estimate is understood in the sense of exponential growth.
Similar calculations can be referenced in Rocha's \cite{R}, Anderson and Rocha's \cite{AW}, and Ruelle's \cite{Ru}.
Therefore, the topological pressure is defined by
$$P(s,r)
=
\lim_{k\to\infty}
\frac1k\log Z_k(s,r;x),$$
and this limit is independent of the initial point $x$.

By Gelfand’s formula for the spectral radius, we have
$$\lambda(s,r)
=
\lim_{k\to\infty}
\|\mathcal L_{s,r}^{\,k}\|^{1/k},$$
where the operator norm is taken in the space of continuous functions. More generally, the spectral radius can be expressed as:
$$\lambda(\delta,r) = \lim_{k\to\infty} \left( \sum_{n_1,\dots,n_k\neq 0} \prod_{i=0}^{k} |f_{n_i}'(x_{i-1})|^{\delta} \right)^{1/k},$$
where $x_{i-1}=f_{n_1}\cdots f_{n_{i-1}}(x_0)$ and the limit is independent of the initial point $x_0.$
Furthermore,  there exists a positive eigenfunction $h$ such that $\mathcal{L}_{\delta,r}h = \lambda(\delta,r)h.$ For the special case of the Hecke groups, we can derive the expression for the spectral radius as
$$\lambda(\delta,r) = 2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{r}{2n}\right)^{2\delta} a_n(\delta,r).$$
and hence
$$P(s,r)=\log\lambda(s,r).$$

In \cite{MU},  Mauldin and Urbanski  showed that for a regular system, the dimension of the limit set is the unique zero of the function $r \mapsto P(\delta(r),r)$, i.e. the Hausdorff dimension is the unique zero of the pressure function with respect to $s.$ Hence we only need to take the unique zero point of the equation $\lambda(\delta(r), r) = 1.$

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
 
                                                                   
Applying the implicit function theorem to $P(\delta(r),r),$  we have  the existence of a unique zero point of the equation $\lambda(\delta(r), r) = 1.$

                                                                                     
 
                                                                                                                           
                     
                                                    
                      
  
                       
                                                        
                      
  
                       
                                   
                 
  
                  
              
                       
                                             

By Lemma 4.3 of this article, since the group $\Gamma _{r} $ contains parabolic elements, hence the regular index is $\theta =1/2.$ We can directly use Lemma 3.2 in \cite{MU} to conclude that $P(s,r)$ is strictly decreasing in the variable $s$ on the interval $\left ( 1/2,+  \infty  \right ) .$
Moreover, by Theorem 1.2 we can conclude that $P(\delta,r)$ is real-analytic in the region $(0,1)\times(1/2,1).$ The real-analytic implicit function theorem implies that there exists a neighborhood $U_{r_0}$ of $r_0$ and a unique real-analytic function
$$\widetilde\delta:U_{r_0}\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$
such that
$$P(\widetilde\delta(r),r)=0,
\qquad
\widetilde\delta(r_0)=s_0.$$

On the other hand, since $P(s,r)$ is strictly decreasing in $s$, the equation
$P(s,r)=0$
has at most one zero for each fixed $r$. Hence,
$\widetilde\delta(r)=\delta(r)$
on $U_{r_0}$. Since $r_0\in(0,1)$ was arbitrary, we conclude that
$r\longmapsto H.\!\dim(\Lambda_r)$
is real-analytic on $(0,1)$.
